title: The Silent Aftermath: Regressed PDR & Chronic Retinal Vein Occlusion
summary: A comprehensive guide to identifying the 'burned-out' or regressed signs of Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) and the sequelae of old Central (CRVO) or Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO). Essential for differentiating benign collaterals from active neovascularization.

sections.title: Definition & Overview of Regression
sections.content: Regression refers to the involutional stage of retinal vascular diseases following treatment (PRP, Anti-VEGF) or natural progression into a 'burned-out' phase. While active signs like hemorrhage subside, permanent structural changes and 'ghost' features remain as diagnostic footprints of past ischemia.

sections.title: Key Signs of Regressed PDR
content: Vascular 'Ghosting': White, thread-like vessels (atrophied NVD/NVE).
Fibrotic Stalks: Opaque, white/grey membranes on the disc or along arcades.
PRP Laser Scars: Pigmented or atrophic circular burns in the mid-periphery.
Tractional Changes: Fixed retinal folds or 'dragged' macula/vessels.
Venous Beading (VB) & Duplication: Residual evidence of severe NPDR prior to PDR conversion.
Arteriolar Narrowing: Significant attenuation of the arterial tree.
Vitreous Condensation: Remnants of old vitreous hemorrhage (Schaffer's sign or 'tobacco dust' is different, but look for old clots).

sections.title: Signs of Old CRVO / BRVO
content: Optociliary Shunt Vessels: Large, tortuous vessels on the disc (CRVO) connecting the retinal and choroidal circulations.
Venous Sheathing: White 'cuffing' around formerly engorged veins.
Collateral Vessels: Tortuous vessels crossing the horizontal raphe (BRVO) or disc (CRVO).
Macular Pigmentary Changes: Mottled RPE from chronic cystoid macular edema (CME).
Secondary ERM: Epiretinal membrane formation over the area of old occlusion.
Segmental Sclerosis: If BRVO, sheathing and narrowing are limited to the affected quadrant.

sections.title: The Great Mimicker: Collaterals vs. NV
Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: 1. Multi-modal Imaging: Start with color fundus photography (CFP).
2. FFA: Identify 'Silent' areas of non-perfusion vs. active leakage.
3. OCT-Angiography: Visualize the Deep Capillary Plexus (DCP) for remodeling.
4. Structural OCT: Look for DRIL (Disorganization of Retinal Inner Layers) and thinning.
5. Gonioscopy: MANDATORY to rule out NVA/NVG even if the fundus looks quiet.

sections.title: Red Flags: Reactivation Signs
content: New 'fuzziness' or blurring of previously sharp fibrotic vessels.
Sudden increase in IOP (check for NVI/NVA).
Recurrent vitreous hemorrhage (could be 'crunch' syndrome or new NV).
New onset of microaneurysms at the edge of old laser scars.

content.explanation: T: Tractional folds, H: Heme (old/hemosiderin), E: Ensheathment, G: Ghost vessels, O: Optociliary shunts, S: Scars (PRP), T: Thinning (Retinal), S: Sclerosis.

sections.title: Landmark Studies Impact
content: ETDRS: Defined PDR regression criteria after PRP.
CVOS/BRAVO: Established the natural history of vein occlusions and the role of grid laser.
Protocol S: Compared Anti-VEGF vs. PRP for PDR, highlighting the 'regression-reactivation' cycle.
SCORE: Defined the prognosis of chronic CME in RVO.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Resident Exams
content: If you see optociliary shunts but no diabetes, think CRVO or Optic Nerve Sheath Meningioma.
Collaterals never leak on FFA; Neovascularization always leaks.
PRP scars 'creep' or enlarge over time (atrophic creep).
The presence of DRIL on OCT is a strong predictor of poor visual recovery even after regression.
